newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: New Moldova leader promises faster market reform.
newsitem.headline: New Moldova leader promises faster market reform.

text.p: Moldovan president-elect Petru Lucinschi, who won a four-year term on a centre-left ticket, reaffirmed on Monday his commitment to speeding up free market reforms and accused allies of the outgoing leader of corruption.
"We need to form a government which will not only continue reforms but accelerate them," Lucinschi told a news conference.

He will take over from President Mircea Snegur on January 15, six weeks after beating him in a bitterly fought election, during which Snegur accused Lucinschi, once a top Kremlin official, of wanting to restore Soviet-style communism.

The president-elect said he would form a government of "professional and honest people", adding that the head of the national audit office, Ion Cebuc, was in the running for the job of premier, to take over from Andrei Sangheli, who has resigned.
Lucinschi, who portrays himself a social democrat, has said he could appoint social democrats, communists and even some right-wing nationalists who supported Snegur in the election.
The latter have rejected such suggestions, however.

Lucinschi, a 56-year-old intellectual who has been chairman of parliament for three years, slammed the paralysis of economic policy over the past year, which was partly a result of a feud between Snegur and the government.
Although his campaign stressed social welfare and more state control over the economy, Lucinschi has since turned his attention to the slow pace of market reforms.
"The national leu currency was stable, inflation and the discount rate were low. But bitter political battles before the poll meant many reforms were delayed," he said.
Lucinschi said that agrarian reform conceived to allow free trade in agricultural land, business privatisation and the restructuring of big Soviet-era plants had fallen behind.
He said gross domestic product (GDP), which fell by three percent in 1995, would shrink another 10 percent this year.
Lucinschi said he would clamp down on corruption.

Snegur supporters have complained of threats and being thrown out of jobs since the election. But the president-elect, clearly annoyed, accused his predecessor's allies of corruption and trying "to steal as much as possible" before he took over.
